newsitem.title: UK: Scotland, Wales hardest hit by stg strength - report.
newsitem.headline: Scotland, Wales hardest hit by stg strength - report.

text.p: Scotland, Wales and the Midlands will be among the hardest hit regions in Britain if sterling remains strong, while London will escape relatively unscathed, according to a report published on Thursday.

"Wales and Scotland suffer because the electronics industry appears vulnerable to a less competitive rate for sterling," independent forecasters Cambridge Econometrics said in their latest edition of Regional Economic Prospects.
"The manufacturing heartland of the West and East Midlands is clearly vulnerable to strong sterling although much of the effect appears only in 1998."
The report said motor vehicles output was less sensitive to a high exchange rate in the short term, and this would delay the impact of sterling's strength on the Midlands.
But the electronics industry in Scotland and Wales would be more immediately affected. "Competition is intense and based increasingly on price in the commoditised end of the market," the report said.

The least affected of Britain's regions would be Greater London, it said. "Its manufacturing base is less important than other regions but its tradeable services...are affected and there are knock-on effects from lower activity elsewhere."
Cambridge Econometrics said its forecasts were based on a scenario where sterling slips back from its present highs to average 2.56 marks in 1997. Sterling currently stands at around 2.74 marks.
Such a scenario would lead to an acceleration of growth this year, it said, with GDP growth forecast at 3.4 percent in 1997 and 2.9 percent in 1998.

"Manufacturing output growth is expected to accelerate sharply in 1997, if sterling falls back from its present high levels, driven by strong consumer demand, a recovery in export demand and an end to reduced stockbuilding."
The South west, London and the West Midlands would enjoy the strongest growth, while the East Midlands and Northern Ireland would underperform the rest of the country, the report said.
